name: The kept lacuna
work: If Not, Winter: Fragments of Sappho
statement: **O1 — The kept lacuna.** *If Not, Winter: Fragments of Sappho* (2002) prints Sappho's fragments with the damage visible: brackets and white space where the papyrus is lost. The gap is set on the page as part of what reaches the reader. Carson's phrase for the brackets: "an aesthetic gesture toward the papyrological event" (Q1, through #625 §4 and #902). The archive reads the absence as "part of the transmission" (#625), sets Carson, who "leaves the wound open", beside a poet who fills the gaps (#562), records that she preserves fragment 31's fragmentary syntax (#337 §6.3) and its fifth-stanza opening (#1054), drawn like every modern edition from one manuscript stemma (#1052). Grade: Q1; archive reading. The Academy calls the book "her interpretation of Sappho's poem fragments" and counts the translations "independent works in their own right"; it says nothing of the gaps. Field: the book is listed (F21).

lost: the papyrus, the damage kept, Sappho

name: The triangle of desire
statement: **O2 — The triangle of desire.** *Eros the Bittersweet* (1986), a reworking of her 1981 doctoral thesis (F11), examines eros as pleasure and pain at once, after Sappho's *glukupikron* (F9), and "considers how triangulations of desire appear in the writings of Sappho, ancient Greek novelists, and Plato" (F10). Her formulation: "Where eros is lack, its activation calls for three structural components — lover, beloved, and that which comes between them" (Q1, through #626 §II). The Academy quotes her "stereoscopic vision" that can "hold in equipoise two perspectives at once" (Q1, through the biobibliography). A philological reading of a fragment becomes an instrument for reading desire. Grade: Q1; field; Academy.
lost: the fragment, lack, pain with sweetness

name: The philologist's procedure carried into the poem
statement: **O3 — The philologist's procedure carried into the poem.** The Academy: "Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist's obsession with words and the poet's desire for new meaning", and she "has herself identified the etymology of words as the starting point for all her work" (Academy). The thesis became an essay that, on John D'Agata's account, "first stunned the classics community as a work of Greek scholarship; then it stunned the nonfiction community … and then, and only then … it finally stunned the poets" (F12). Her books blend poetry, essay, prose, criticism, translation, dramatic dialogue, fiction and non-fiction (F8). The field records the dispute this produces: Kirsch, "The writing is clearly prose" (F34); D'Agata, how prosaic a poem can be "before it becomes something else altogether" (F35). Grade: Academy; field.

name: The received figure given the whole book
statement: **O4 — The received figure given the whole book.** *Autobiography of Red* (1998) takes as its starting point Stesichoros's fragments on the red winged Geryon, whom Herakles kills in his tenth labour for his cattle (F32; Academy). Carson "recasts the terrifying giant as a tender 'hero' devoted to his mother, in what becomes a modern Bildungsroman" (Academy); "In Carson, Herakles breaks Geryon's heart and steals his innocence" (Kirsch, F33). The figure at the edge of a hero's labour is given the whole book as its life. Grade: field; Academy; the Stesichorean base to read.
grade: field; Academy; the Stesichorean base to read.
lost: Stesichoros, Geryon, the life told whole
caution: **Caution on O4.** The surviving fragments of Stesichoros's *Geryoneis* already give Geryon speech and pathos, his mother pleading with him (Q2, a reader's report of 8 October; to read: the fragments). O4 is stated at what Carson adds: the figure becomes the book's centre and its life is told whole. If a reading of the fragments finds that they already give Geryon a whole life, O4 is revised.

name: The change of carrier
statement: **O5 — The change of carrier.** *Nox* (2010), made in 2000 as an epitaph for her brother (F23), is "a creation as sculptural as it is literary, an epitaph in the form of a box containing an accordion-fold-out of pictures, letters and other written texts", with Catullus's elegy 101 for his brother and "Carson's moving translation of the poem" (Academy); its design and performance were done with Robert Currie (F24). The elegy is set in the object that carries it, and the ancient elegy for a brother is carried inside the modern one. Grade: Academy; field; attested by the author, who read the object in his own copy (the box, the fold-out, Catullus 101 and its translation "all check out", 8 October 2026; the copy is no longer held). Pointer: the conclusion of the author's 2013 dissertation, *Strange New Canons*, treats *Nox* (#921 §2.7 reports the pairing with "Snub-Poemed"); it is unread in this round and enters O5 as an archive reading when read.

name: The translation as the fragment's vehicle
statement: 3.2 **R1 — The translation as the fragment's vehicle.** Fragment 147's contemporary circulation "is overwhelmingly Carson-mediated" (*If Not, Winter*: "someone will remember us / I say / even in another time"), in epigraphs, memorial culture and reflective sites, and the AI Overview's remembrance card composes from that register (#1548 §6; Q1, documented from the search surface). It is an operation of a different kind: performed by the work in other hands, after it left the author's, and kept apart from O1–O5 for that reason. It has a twin in this object: Carson's translation carries Sappho, keeping the gap; the motivation now carries Carson (§5.3).
kept_at_motivation_grain: a relation to translation, at most
lost: fragment 147, Carson's English as its carrier

name: the relation the work bears to the classical tradition
statement: Of the five compositional operations, four are addressed to the classical text at a different stage of its transmission: kept damaged (O1), read into a structure of desire (O2), given a whole book (O4), carried inside another elegy and its object (O5). The fifth carries the philologist's procedure into the poem (O3). The relation the work bears to the classical tradition, on this specification, is to the text *as transmitted*: quoted, damaged, lost, translated, and surviving in the form of its survival.
